analysis.one_liner: Gives courts and copyright holders power to cut off foreign 'pirate' websites' ads, payments, and US access.
analysis.headline: The bill never reached a House floor vote; after hearings and two markup sessions in the Judiciary Committee, the 112th Congress ended without passing it.
analysis.plain_summary: SOPA would have let the Attorney General, and in some cases private copyright holders, get court orders to cut foreign websites off from American internet users, ad services, and payment companies. It would have made unauthorized streaming of copyrighted works a crime when the retail value topped $1,000 within six months, and it expanded criminal penalties for trafficking in counterfeit goods, including counterfeit drugs and goods falsely marked as meeting military standards. Internet providers, search engines, payment networks, and ad services would have been legally required to block or defund sites named in orders, generally within five days.
analysis.who_benefits: Large copyright holders — film studios, record labels, and other owners of movies, music, and software — gain the most: a private notice system to cut off a website's payment and advertising revenue without a full lawsuit, a new felony for streaming, and heavier penalties for counterfeit goods. The government also gains new enforcement tools, including dedicated intellectual property officers in embassies abroad.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Film studios, record labels, copyright holders

how_it_helps.text: Copyright holders can send a written notice to payment processors and ad networks requiring them to cut off a site's revenue within five days; the site must file a counter-notification or lose its services, and the right holder can then seek an injunction in court [S2].

The Attorney General can sue foreign websites used for piracy and obtain orders requiring US internet providers to block subscribers' access, search engines to remove links, and payment and ad networks to refuse service [S2][S3].

Unauthorized public performance of copyrighted works by digital transmission becomes a federal crime when at least 10 performances occur in a 180-day period and the total retail value exceeds $1,000 [S3].
Penalties rise for trafficking in counterfeit drugs and in goods falsely identified as meeting military or national security standards, up to 20 years for individuals [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Ordinary internet users bear the risk of overblocking: the notice-and-shutoff system lets a copyright holder defund a site before any judge reviews the claim, with only a counter-notification as protection. Internet companies — providers, search engines, payment networks, ad networks, and domain operators — absorb compliance costs and the threat of court action if they fail to comply on time.

drawbacks.text: The private enforcement system lets a right holder cut off a site's payments and advertising on its own written notice; the site's only immediate remedy is a counter-notification, which a foreign operator must pair with consent to US court jurisdiction — a concession many operators will not make [S2][S3].

Making streaming a crime at a $1,000 retail-value threshold and ten performances in six months criminalizes activity many Americans treat as ordinary sharing, and the bill instructs the Sentencing Commission to add enhancements, including for offenses tied to organized enterprises [S3].

Service providers, search engines, payment networks, and ad services must take blocking or defunding measures within five days of being served a court order, and the Attorney General can sue companies that knowingly fail to comply or that offer tools to bypass the blocks — a compliance burden and liability risk for the companies that operate the internet [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets real harms — foreign piracy sites and counterfeit drugs that genuinely endanger buyers — and its counterfeit-goods provisions are the strongest part. But the headline mechanism inverts the usual process: it defunds websites first and adjudicates later, on a low criminal threshold for streaming, and it conscripts the companies that run the internet into enforcing it under threat of suit. For the cost to everyday internet use and to the tech industry, the narrow benefit to copyright enforcement does not carry the weight, which is why even many of the bill's early supporters abandoned it.

outcome.mechanism: The House Judiciary Committee held hearings and two markup sessions, but the bill was never brought to a vote on the House floor, and the 112th Congress ended with it dead.

narrative.text: Rep. Lamar Smith of Texas introduced the bill on October 26, 2011 with a bipartisan group of original cosponsors, including Reps. Conyers, Berman, Goodlatte, Blackburn, and Schiff [S1][S3].

The bill was referred to the House Judiciary Committee on introduction, then to its Intellectual Property subcommittee; the full committee held a hearing on November 16, 2011, discharged the subcommittee, and held markup sessions on December 15 and 16, 2011 [S5].

The bill gathered 31 cosponsors — 16 of 190 House Democrats and 15 of 239 House Republicans — but no action after the December 16, 2011 markup appears in the record, and it never received a House floor vote before the Congress ended on January 3, 2013 [S1][S4][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Internet users and internet companies came out ahead: the defunding-and-blocking regime never took effect, and the copyright industries gained no new tools. The bill's backers, including the film and music industries that pressed for it, gained nothing from the outcome.

for.name: Rep. Lamar Smith
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, gathered bipartisan cosponsors, and as Judiciary chairman held a full-committee hearing and two markup sessions on it in December 2011.

against.name: Wikipedia, Google, and other major websites
against.what_they_did: In January 2012 staged a widely covered day of protest, including Wikipedia's blackout of its English-language site, warning the bill would break the open internet.

against.name: Millions of internet users
against.what_they_did: Delivered a wave of petitions, calls, and emails to Congress during the January 2012 protest, prompting many cosponsors to withdraw their support.

against.name: President Obama's administration
against.what_they_did: Publicly announced in January 2012 that it would not support legislation that encourages censorship or disrupts the internet's underlying architecture.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship split almost evenly across parties — 16 of 190 House Democrats and 15 of 239 House Republicans — and the opposition that killed the bill also crossed party lines rather than splitting on them.

industries.industry: Motion picture and music industries (major copyright holders)
industries.note: The bill hands them a private notice system to cut off websites' payment and ad revenue without first proving the case in court, plus a new streaming felony. Their gain is paid for by tighter control over what ordinary users can access and share online.

industries.industry: Internet companies (providers, search engines, social platforms, domain operators)
industries.note: The bill makes them responsible for blocking access and removing links on five days' notice, with liability exposure if they fail or if they enable bypass tools. Their interest in defeating it ran alongside users' interest in an open internet.

industries.industry: Payment networks and online advertising services
industries.note: They must suspend services to named sites within five days of a notice or court order, but the bill grants them immunity for doing so. They opposed the bill publicly alongside the internet industry.

New trafficking offenses and immunity for cutting off sites selling counterfeit or no-prescription drugs serve its anti-counterfeiting interests. Some of that protects consumers from dangerous fake medicine, though the same enforcement tools also entrench the industry's control over online drug sales.
The bill targets foreign domain names directly and exposes registries and registrars to court orders blocking resolution. They joined the internet industry's opposition.
